title: Help and discovery
lead: Use man, --help, which, type, find and history to research an unfamiliar command on your own, without the internet.
objectives: You open a man page, navigate it, search it and quit; you recognise the section numbers (1, 5, 8).
You get a quick summary with --help and help, and read SYNOPSIS notation ([ ], | and ...).
You find where a command is and what type it is with which and type, and search for files with find.
You review old commands with history and systematically resolve 'command not found' errors (exit code 127).

sections.title: man: manual pages
body: Linux has hundreds of commands; even professionals don't memorise them all, they **know where to look**. The most reliable source is the system's own manual, the `man` pages: `man ls`.

The page opens in a pager: **Space** goes down a page, **b** goes up, **/kernel** + Enter searches the text, **n** jumps to the next match, **q** quits. Page headings are always the same: NAME (short name), SYNOPSIS (usage form), DESCRIPTION, OPTIONS, EXAMPLES, SEE ALSO.

The manual is split into **sections**: 1 = user commands, 5 = file formats (e.g. `/etc/passwd`), 8 = administration commands. The same name can appear in several sections: `man passwd` shows the command, `man 5 passwd` shows the file format. In the simulator the pages are short and section numbers are not supported; on a real VM you see the full page.

commands.what: Opens the manual page of a command.
commands.where: When learning a new command or option.
commands.why: It is accurate information that ships with your system and matches its version.

commands.what: Opens a specific manual section.
commands.where: When the same name is both a command and a file format.
commands.why: You reach the right page directly.

commands.what: Gives a one-line description of a command.
commands.where: To quickly remember what a command does.
commands.why: You get a summary without opening the page.

commands.what: Searches manual pages by keyword.
commands.where: When you don't know the command's name but know what it does.
commands.why: Searching for 'copy file' lets you find cp.

sections.tip: If you get lost in a page, leave with `q`. To search, type `/`, enter the word, press Enter; the next match is `n`.
sections.warn: `whatis` and `apropos` rely on an index (mandb); on freshly installed minimal systems they may return nothing. In that case run `sudo mandb`.

sections.title: --help and help: quick summary
body: If you don't want to read the whole manual, `ls --help` prints a short usage summary. If the output is long, limit it with `| head` or `| less`: `ls --help | head -n 5`.

**Shell built-in** commands like `cd` have no separate program, so `man cd` sometimes doesn't exist. For them Bash has the `help` command: `help cd`. On its own, `help` lists the known commands (in the simulator this list is short).
Quick rule: for an external program use `--help` first, `man` for details; for a shell built-in use `help`.

commands.what: Prints a short usage summary of the command.
commands.where: To quickly recall an option.
commands.why: It is much faster than man.

commands.what: Gives help about Bash's own (built-in) commands.
commands.where: For commands like cd, type, history.
commands.why: These commands may not have a separate man page.

commands.what: Shows long output page by page.
commands.where: For long --help or file output.
commands.why: The navigation keys are the same as in man.

sections.tip: When help is printed, don't miss the top line: the `Usage:` line gives you the usage form.

sections.title: Reading SYNOPSIS notation
body: The SYNOPSIS line gives the command's 'pattern'. Example: `ls [OPTION]... [FILE]...`. Read it like this:

Anything inside `[ ]` is **optional**. `...` means the previous part can be written **more than once**. `a | b` means **either a or b**. `< >` or UPPERCASE (FILE, DIR) is a value you substitute. Parts written in bold are typed exactly as shown.
Example: `cp [OPTION]... SOURCE... DEST` → options are optional, at least one source and one destination are required. `ls` also works with no arguments because everything is in square brackets.

commands.what: Shows the usage pattern (Usage).
commands.where: To learn the order of arguments.
commands.why: If you can read the pattern, you can figure out any new command.

commands.what: Opens the page that contains the SYNOPSIS section.
commands.where: A simple example to practise with.
commands.why: You see square brackets and ... in a real page.

sections.tip: To find what is mandatory, look at the parts outside the square brackets.

sections.title: which and type: where is the command?
body: When you type a command, the shell searches the directories in the `PATH` variable in order. `which ls` prints the **path** it finds (e.g. `/usr/bin/ls`).

`type` is more informative: it tells you whether the command is an **external program**, a **shell built-in (builtin)**, an alias or a function. `type cd` → `cd is a shell builtin`. Use it to understand which one runs when several commands share the same name.
To see the contents of `PATH`, use `echo $PATH`. `alias` and `command -v` also work on a real VM, but not in the simulator.

commands.what: Shows the file path of the command.
commands.where: To find out where a program is installed.
commands.why: You verify that you are running the right version.

commands.what: Tells the type of the command (program, builtin, alias).
commands.where: When investigating unexpected behaviour.
commands.why: You tell a builtin from an external program.

commands.what: Prints the directories where commands are searched.
commands.where: When investigating 'command not found'.
commands.why: You see whether the program's directory is in PATH.

commands.what: Prints the path/name if the command exists; stays silent otherwise.
commands.where: In scripts, to check 'is it installed?'.
commands.why: It is a portable existence check.

commands.what: Lists defined shortcuts.
commands.where: To understand where commands like `ll` come from.
commands.why: You see the source of what type calls an 'alias'.

sections.tip: If a command behaves strangely, first check its type with `type command`.

sections.title: find: file search basics
body: `find <start> <conditions>` walks a directory tree and prints what matches the conditions. The two most common conditions: `-name` (by name) and `-type` (`f` file, `d` directory).

Put the wildcard **in quotes**: `find . -name "*.txt"`. Without quotes the shell expands the pattern itself first and the result is misleading. The start point `.` is the current directory, `~` is home.
You can count the result with `| wc -l` and save it with `> file`. `-maxdepth 1` limits the depth on a real system (the simulator ignores it).

commands.what: Searches the directory tree for files matching a condition.
commands.where: When you forgot where a file is.
commands.why: It scans the tree by name, type or size.

commands.what: Finds only files (f) or directories (d).
commands.where: To count directories separately.
commands.why: You narrow the result.

commands.what: Gives the number of items found.
commands.where: To know how many matches there are.
commands.why: You get a number without reading a long list.

sections.tip: To hide error messages on a real system, add `2>/dev/null`.
sections.warn: Don't delete with `find ... -delete` or `-exec rm`; first view the list with plain `find`, then decide.

sections.title: history: past commands
body: `history` lists the commands you typed in this and earlier sessions with numbers. If it is long, take the last ten commands with `history | tail -n 10`.

In real Bash, **up arrow** brings back the previous command, **Ctrl+R** searches the history, `!!` re-runs the last command, `!42` re-runs command number 42. The simulator does not support `!!`; the arrow keys work.
Commands that contain secrets (passwords) are written to the history; don't forget that.

commands.what: Lists past commands with numbers.
commands.where: To remember what you typed earlier.
commands.why: You find a long command without retyping it.

commands.what: Shows only the most recent commands.
commands.where: In a long history.
commands.why: The list stays short.

commands.what: Re-runs the last command.
commands.where: `sudo !!` for a privileged retry.
commands.why: It saves time.

sections.tip: Press Ctrl+R and type part of the command: Bash brings back the match.

sections.title: Dealing with 'command not found'
body: If you type a command that doesn't exist you get `nosuchcmd: command not found` and the exit code is **127**: `nosuchcmd; echo $?` → `127`. Code 127 means 'command not found'.

Systematic check: (1) Is it a typo? (`ls` instead of `lss`) (2) Upper/lower case: Linux is case-sensitive. (3) Check whether it exists with `type command`. (4) If the program isn't installed, install the package (Ubuntu `sudo apt install`, Rocky/Alma `sudo dnf install`). (5) If it is installed, check the directory with `echo $PATH`.
This differs from the 'No such file or directory' error: there the command was found but the file you gave doesn't exist.

commands.what: Prints the exit code of the last command.
commands.where: When checking whether a command succeeded.
commands.why: 0 means success, 127 means command not found.

commands.what: Does the command exist, and where?
commands.where: The first check after an error.
commands.why: It weeds out typos.

sections.tip: On a real system Ubuntu sometimes suggests 'Command 'x' not found, did you mean...'; read the suggestion carefully.

t01.text: Open the manual page of the `ls` command with `man ls`.
t01.hint: The sim page is short; look at NAME, SYNOPSIS and DESCRIPTION.

t02.text: Show the short usage summary with `ls --help`.

t03.text: Type `type cd`. Does the output say 'builtin'? What does that mean?
t03.hint: Builtin: inside Bash, not a separate program.

t04.text: Find the path of the `ls` command with `which ls`.

t05.text: Open `man cat` and read the SYNOPSIS line: which part is optional?
t05.hint: Anything inside square brackets is optional.

t06.text: Type `help` and see the list of known commands.

t07.text: Find all `.txt` files under the current directory with `find . -name "*.txt"`.

t08.text: List the commands you have typed so far with `history`.

t09.text: Show only the first three lines of the page with `man ls | head -n 3`.

t10.text: Predict: what number does `nosuchcmd; echo $?` print? Then run it to verify.

t11.text: Predict: how many directories does `find ~ -type d | wc -l` count under home (including home)? Run it and verify.
t11.hint: Desktop, Documents, Downloads and home itself.

t12.text: Debug: `man mkdirr` gives an error ('No manual entry'). Open the manual of the correct command with `man mkdir`.

t13.text: Mini: find where the `todo.txt` file is with `find` and save the path to the file `~/path.txt`.

t14.text: Challenge: In a single command, count the `.txt` files under home and write the number to `~/count.txt`.
t14.hint: `find`, pipe, `wc -l` and redirection. The result is the file count; .txt files you created yourself are counted too.

t15.text: TICKET #4410 — Support: 'Where is ls installed, and what kind of command is cd?' Save the path to `~/ls_path.txt` and the type of `cd` to `~/cd_type.txt`.

t16.text: TICKET #4411 — The teacher wants to see what you tried: first run `which ls`, then save the history to `~/hist.txt`.

vm.intro: Run the following commands on your VM (Ubuntu, Rocky, Alma or WSL). There is no destructive command; still, remember to leave the pager (man) with `q`.

v01.title: Open a manual page
v01.text: Open `man ls`, search for `long` with `/`, leave with `q`. Then paste the first lines.

blocks.expected:
LS(1)    User Commands

NAME
       ls - list directory contents

differs: If your language is Turkish/German the headings may be translated.
If you get 'No manual entry', the manual package is missing: `sudo apt install man-db` or `sudo dnf install man-db`.

v02.title: --help summary
v02.text: Paste the first lines of the `ls --help` output.

blocks.expected:
Usage: ls [OPTION]... [FILE]...
List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).

differs: On macOS or BusyBox the `--help` format may differ; run it on a Linux VM.

v03.title: Command types
v03.text: Paste the type and path of the `cd`, `ls` and `which ls` commands.

blocks.cmd:
type cd
type ls
which ls
blocks.expected:
cd is a shell builtin
ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto'
/usr/bin/ls

differs: `ls` may be an alias (for colour on Ubuntu/Rocky); this is normal.
On some distributions you get `/bin/ls` (`/bin` is linked to `/usr/bin`).

v04.title: Search with find
v04.text: Find the `.txt` files in your home. Since the output is personal, just say 'Done'.
differs: If there is no output, you have no .txt files in your home: first create one with `touch ~/notes.txt`.

v05.title: whatis and apropos
v05.text: Search for the one-line description of `ls` and for commands containing 'copy'.

blocks.expected:
ls (1) - list directory contents
cp (1) - copy files and directories

differs: If you see 'nothing appropriate', there is no index: run `sudo mandb` and try again.
On Ubuntu/Rocky the `apropos` output may have a different number of lines.

v06.title: command not found
v06.text: Run a command that doesn't exist and paste the exit code.
differs: Ubuntu may suggest 'Command 'nosuchcmd' not found, did you mean...'; the last line should still be 127.
If you use Zsh the message is 'zsh: command not found: nosuchcmd'.

v07.title: Look at the history
differs: The numbers will be different; this is normal.
In a freshly opened terminal the list may be short.

v08.title: Manual sections
v08.text: Open the section 5 page describing the format of the `/etc/passwd` file and paste the first lines.

blocks.expected:
PASSWD(5)   File Formats Manual

NAME
       passwd - password file

differs: `man passwd` (section 1) is a different page: the password-changing command.
If the page is missing, the `man-db` or `man-pages` package is absent.

q1.q: Which keys are used to search for text in a man page and to quit the page?
q1.explain: `/word` searches, `n` goes to the next match, `q` quits.

q2.q: In the pattern `ls [OPTION]... [FILE]...`, what do `[ ]` and `...` mean?
options: The part in square brackets is hidden
Optional and can be written more than once
q2.explain: Square brackets mean optional, the three dots show that the previous part can be repeated.

q3.q: What is the number in the output of `nosuchcmd; echo $?`?
q3.explain: In the 'command not found' case Bash returns 127 as the exit code.

q4.q: With which command do you see that `cd` is not an external program?
q4.explain: The output of `type cd` is `cd is a shell builtin`; that is, it is inside Bash.

summary: `man command` is the detailed manual, `command --help` a short summary, `help` is for shell built-ins.
In man: `/` searches, `n` next, `q` quits; sections: 1 commands, 5 file formats, 8 administration.
`which` shows the path, `type` shows the type; `find . -name "*.txt"` searches for files.
`history` lists the past; `command not found` has exit code 127.

glossary.meaning: The manual page of a command that ships with the system.
The man section showing the command's usage pattern.
A command embedded in Bash that has no separate program.
The list of directories where commands are searched.
The number a command leaves when it finishes; 0 is success, 127 is command not found.
A program that shows long text page by page (less).
